description: ग़ usually represents a voiced velar or uvular fricative [ɣ], somewhat like a voiced version of the sound in Scottish “loch,” but made farther back in the mouth. It is not the ordinary Hindi ग [g]. In everyday Hindi, many speakers pronounce ग़ like ग, so both ग़ज़ल and गज़ल may be heard with a plain “g” sound. To make the distinct sound, raise the back of the tongue near the soft palate and let the breath create friction while keeping the vocal cords vibrating.

thoughts: English speakers are very familiar with the /f/ pronunciation. The main Hindi-specific point is that फ़ is the dotted letter used to represent /f/, distinguishing it from फ, which traditionally represents aspirated /pʰ/, although the distinction is not always maintained in everyday speech.
description: फ़ is usually pronounced /f/, like the sound in English “fan” or “coffee”: place your upper teeth lightly on your lower lip and let air pass through. In some Hindi speech, especially with older or strongly Sanskritized pronunciation, it may be pronounced closer to aspirated /pʰ/—like a strongly puffed “p”—but /f/ is the normal pronunciation in familiar borrowed words.

thoughts: English speakers are likely to recognize the general idea of an r-like sound, and many American speakers already produce a similar tap in words such as “butter.” However, Hindi र is normally a deliberate tongue tap rather than the usual English r, so the exact articulation may require practice.
description: र is usually pronounced as a quick tongue tap, similar to the sound many American English speakers make for the middle consonant in “butter” or “water.” Briefly touch the tongue against the ridge just behind the upper teeth; do not use the English bunched or retroflex-like r. In careful or emphatic speech, it may be slightly trilled, especially when doubled or in a consonant cluster.

thoughts: English has the ordinary n sound, but not usually this retroflex version as a separate sound. Learners may initially pronounce ण like English n; curling the tongue tip slightly backward helps produce the Hindi sound.
description: ण is usually pronounced as a retroflex “n” [ɳ]. Curl the tip of your tongue slightly backward so it touches the roof of your mouth farther back than English n, then release through the nose. In everyday Hindi, some speakers pronounce it closer to an ordinary n, especially in Sanskrit-derived words.

description: न is normally a voiced dental nasal, like the n in English “nice,” but with the tongue touching the back of the upper front teeth rather than the gum ridge. It can occur at the beginning, middle, or end of a word. In fast speech, its exact tongue position may be slightly influenced by a neighboring consonant, but learners should use a clear dental n.

thoughts: English speakers almost certainly know this sound from English. The main point is to keep the lips fully closed and pronounce the m distinctly wherever it occurs, including at the end of a Hindi word.
description: म is the ordinary Hindi “m” sound, like the m in English “mother” or “man.” It is a voiced bilabial nasal: close both lips and let the voice resonate through the nose. Unlike English, Hindi may pronounce it clearly at the end of a word rather than weakening or changing it. Before another consonant, it can be slightly assimilated to that consonant, but the basic sound remains an m.

thoughts: English speakers are very familiar with the [ŋ] sound from words such as “sing,” but may not recognize it as a separate consonant letter. description: ङ represents the “ng” sound [ŋ], like the sound at the end of English “sing” or in the middle of “finger” when pronounced without a hard g. In Hindi it normally occurs before velar sounds such as ग or क, often in conjuncts like ङ्ग. It is not usually pronounced as a separate “n” followed by “g”; hold the back of the tongue against the soft palate, as for k, but let air pass through the nose. In everyday Hindi spelling, this sound is often written with anusvara (ं) instead of the distinct letter ङ.

thoughts: English speakers may recognize this as similar to the “ny” sound in “canyon,” but the standalone palatal nasal is uncommon in English. In Hindi, the letter is most often encountered inside conjuncts such as ञ्च and ज्ञ, whose pronunciation is highly dependent on the word and speaker.
description: ञ is the palatal nasal, like the “ny” sound in “canyon” or Spanish ñ, pronounced with the middle of the tongue against the hard palate. In modern Hindi it is rarely pronounced by itself: before च/छ it often represents a nasal sound assimilated to the following consonant, as in पञ्च (usually pronounced पंच, roughly “panch”). In the common conjunct ज्ञ, pronunciation varies by region and word; ज्ञान is commonly pronounced “gyaan,” while more careful or Sanskrit-influenced speech may preserve a sound closer to “jnyaan.”

thoughts: English speakers are unlikely to recognize this consonant cluster as a single Hindi sound. thoughts: English speakers are likely to recognize “sh” and “r” separately, and may know “Shri” or “Sri Lanka,” but the Hindi conjunct श्र requires blending them without inserting a vowel between the two consonants. Its pronunciation is commonly “shr,” with variations from a clearly tapped r to a lighter r-like sound.
description: श्र is usually pronounced as a consonant cluster like English “sh” followed immediately by a light tapped or rolled “r”: roughly “shr.” The vowel comes afterward, so श्री is approximately “shree,” while श्रद्धा begins “shrad-.” Do not pronounce it as English “s” + “r”; keep the tongue position for “sh” and move quickly into the “r.” In some Hindi speech, the cluster may sound slightly lighter or closer to “sr,” but the careful pronunciation is “shr.”

thoughts: English speakers may recognize the breathy h-like quality, but the visarga is not a regular English spelling pattern. Its pronunciation is especially noticeable in Sanskrit-derived Hindi vocabulary and may assimilate to a following consonant.
description: The visarga (ः) is a breathy release after a vowel, somewhat like a very light English “h” added at the end of the syllable. In Hindi and Sanskrit-derived words, its sound often changes according to what follows: before a voiceless consonant it may sound like extra aspiration, as in दुःख, pronounced roughly “dukh”; before श it may sound like “h” plus “sh,” as in निःशुल्क. In everyday Hindi, it is sometimes weakened or omitted.

thoughts: English speakers may recognize nasal sounds such as the [m] in “symphony” or [ŋ] in “sing,” but Hindi uses one written mark for several context-dependent nasal pronunciations. The nasalized-vowel pronunciation is less familiar and may require practice.
description: The mark ं (anusvāra) indicates nasalization, and its exact sound depends on what follows. Before a consonant, it often sounds like the nasal consonant made in the same place: [ŋ] before k/g (as in “sing”), [m] before p/b, and [n] before t/d or j. In many common words, especially before certain consonants or at the end, it may instead nasalize the preceding vowel, somewhat like the vowel in French “bon.” Do not pronounce it as a separate full syllable.

thoughts: English speakers are generally familiar with consonant-plus-r clusters such as pr, kr, and tr. The main adjustment is keeping the Hindi r short and avoiding an extra vowel between the consonants; त्र may require a more distinctly dental t than the English tr sound.

thoughts: English speakers are very familiar with the basic /l/ sound and with consonant-plus-l clusters. The main adjustment is to avoid inserting a vowel between the consonants; the Devanagari pattern ्ल explicitly joins the preceding consonant to l.

It is similar to the clusters in English “class,” “plastic,” and “blue.”

thoughts: English speakers are familiar with some similar clusters, especially sm in “small” and tm or dm across syllable boundaries. The Hindi spelling explicitly joins the consonants, and pronunciation can be challenging because learners may insert a short vowel before म.

thoughts: English speakers know /n/ well, but usually not as part of these consonant clusters without an intervening vowel. The doubled-n pronunciation in अन्न is relatively familiar, while clusters such as /ʃn/ in प्रश्न and /ɡn/ in अग्नि require more practice.

thoughts: English speakers may recognize individual consonants such as k, p, f, and t, but Hindi clusters containing dental त are less familiar. The main challenge is pronouncing the consonants consecutively without inserting a vowel, while placing त against the upper teeth.
description: ्त is the conjunct formed when a consonant is followed by dental त without a vowel between them. thoughts: English speakers are generally familiar with an “nd”-like consonant cluster, but Hindi’s dental द is slightly different from the usual English d, and the cluster must be pronounced without adding a vowel between its consonants.

For example, न् + द is pronounced roughly like “nd” in “Hindi,” without inserting an extra vowel between the consonants. In careful Sanskrit-derived pronunciation, the cluster is clearly articulated; in casual speech, the first consonant may be very brief.
